video.title: How to Make $1.6K/Day on Facebook Marketplace

summary: Chris Koerner interviews Matt (Jackson, Michigan), a former high school math teacher who started flipping couches, appliances and church pews on Facebook Marketplace/Craigslist, then moved to riding and zero-turn lawnmowers. He claims $20-30K profit in his first summer, quit teaching, built a helper network (drivers, a mechanic, 'Family of Flippers'), sourced volume from dealers who dislike used stock, and now runs a Toro/Bad Boy etc. equipment dealership with a best month of $1.1M. The episode is heavy on tactics: speed to lead, deposits, negotiation (make the seller name the number first), outsourcing driving first, and calling dealers for under-advertised used inventory. Key takeaway: the edge is buying underpriced at speed and selling at market value, not fixing items.

tactics.name: Win on speed and lock the deal
steps: Monitor listings and respond within minutes
Get the seller on the phone, not text
Pay a deposit via Venmo/PayPal to secure the deal
Ask them to confirm their word is good

quote.text: give them a deposit on Venmo, PayPal, any of those sorts of things, and that will absolutely secure the deal.
quote.speaker: Matt

tactics.name: Outsource driving before negotiating
steps: Do the first 5-10 deals yourself
Negotiate and agree a price by phone first
Send a low-skill driver at $20-25/hr (more if their truck)
Build a call list of 4-5 backups
Have the driver use an inspection sheet and call you to renegotiate if needed

tactics.name: Negotiate: make the seller name the number
steps: Build rapport by talking up the machine
Ask what the lowest price they'd consider is
If they won't say, offer an unrealistically low number
Stay silent after their number
Deliver or other perks only after price

tactics.name: Source from dealers who dislike used stock
steps: Call local dealers asking if they have used units
Find ones not advertising inventory well
Buy their best units, ask what else they have
Become a regular contact for trade-ins

quote.text: There are dealers that just hate dealing with used stuff.
quote.speaker: Matt

tactics.name: Test, don't fix
steps: Choose items that can be fully tested (blades on, drives forward and back)
Buy near perfect condition at low price
Sell at market within a week

tactics.name: Be transparent about being a buyer-seller
steps: Don't hide that you trade
Use wording like a dealer/trade buyer instead of 'flip'
Follow up with past sellers for repeat deals and referrals

warnings.warning: Speed matters: a good deal is gone minutes later, and without a deposit another buyer can offer more.
Flipping items needing repair or doing the fixing yourself lowers hourly return and prevents scaling.
Trailers must be hitched with safety chains; Matt's first trailer detached on a highway.

quote.text: of course there's no safety chance, right?
quote.speaker: Matt

warnings.warning: Sold appliance with a faulty heating element made him doubt the work; avoid selling untested goods.
Don't spend your time hauling; eight hours a day in the car is unsustainable.
Pricing above market (Koerner's mower listed at $3,500 for weeks) means it won't sell.

lessons.lesson: The edge in flipping is buying below market, not repairing; the value is in the buy price.
Outsource the lowest-skill, most time-consuming task (driving) first and keep negotiation for yourself until it is systemised.
Higher-ticket items take the same time and skill but yield bigger margins, so move up the price ladder (couch to mower to equipment).

quote.text: 15% of 2500 bucks is a lot better than 15% of 300 bucks.
quote.speaker: Matt

lessons.lesson: One reliable supplier relationship (a dealer) can provide volume leverage rather than hunting deals one by one.
Take 80% of the profit and move stock fast rather than maximising each sale.

quote.text: You try to make 80% of the money and move it within a week
quote.speaker: Matt

lessons.lesson: Entering a new market, a first purchase is a near no-brainer win because you know the price was off against your outside view; learn by doing.
Pay people market rates and use a trusted network; your time is worth more than DIY tasks.
The niche matters less than picking something with real demand and sticking with it for years.
Business evolves: a side flip became a profit-share programme and then a dealership via opportunistic real estate.

evidence_quality.rationale: First-hand operator with some specific numbers (30 mowers, $20-30K, $1.1M best month, margins) but few verifiable details and inconsistent framing of the $50K month; transcript is auto-caption with garbles.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Matt promotes his How Equipment dealership and YouTube channel; Beehiiv sponsor read from host.
